articles.title: Archaeologists find earliest physical evidence of brass-making in East Asia in southern China
articles.summary: China News: A set of ancient crucibles found in Guangzhou is giving archaeologists new clues about how brass-making technology may have reached medieval China. Th.
articles.body: A set of ancient crucibles found in Guangzhou is giving archaeologists new clues about how brass-making technology may have reached medieval China. The vessels came from an official metallurgical workshop at the Royal Palace of the Nanyue Kingdom and dated from the ninth and tenth centuries AD. Their metal residues show that craftspeople were producing brass locally through cementation rather than simply working with imported objects. According to a research article published by Cambridge University Press, titled ‘Brass technology transmission via maritime routes: crucible evidence from southern China’, points towards wider technological connections with the Islamic world. Guangzhou was a major trading port, and the authors suggest maritime routes may have helped move metallurgical knowledge across regions. The study analysed crucibles using chemical, microscopic and lead-isotope methods. Together, the findings provide direct archaeological evidence for medieval brass production in southern China and offer clues about how the technology may have travelled.Ancient crucibles reveal early brass-making in medieval ChinaArchaeologists found three well-preserved brass-making crucibles at an official metallurgical workshop in Guangzhou. The workshop was part of the Royal Palace of the Nanyue Kingdom site and was active across many centuries. The three crucibles belong to the ninth–tenth century group. Each was cup-shaped with a slightly inward-sloping rim and a rounded base. Some had a pouring spout. They measured about 60-80 mm across and 60-70 mm high, with a capacity of roughly 0.2-0.3 litres. Researchers found heavy heat damage and glassy material on their surfaces. Metal residues inside included copper, zinc compounds and brass droplets. A nearby semi-subterranean furnace also dates to the seventh-tenth centuries. Together, these remains provide direct evidence of metalworking at the site.How did ancient craftspeople make brass from copper and zincThe crucial evidence came from residues left inside the crucibles. Microscopic and chemical analyses identified zinc oxide, zinc silicate, and droplets of brass. One group of crucibles contained high-purity copper and binary brass droplets with about 11-17% zinc. Another contained bronze with tin alongside zinc and produced a copper-zinc-tin alloy. The researchers interpret these residues as evidence for cementation. In this process, zinc-bearing material is heated with copper or a copper alloy so zinc enters the metal and forms brass. The remains therefore show more than the presence of finished brass objects. They preserve traces of the production process itself.How did brass-making technology reach medieval GuangzhouThe study also examined lead isotopes to investigate the likely origin of the raw materials. The three analysed crucibles had similar lead-isotope ratios that fit signatures associated with the Cathaysia tectonic province. Because these signatures occur widely across southern China, the researchers say a local source for the raw materials is reasonable. The technology itself may have travelled from farther west. The authors point to similarities between the Guangzhou crucibles and brass-making vessels associated with the Islamic world. Guangzhou was also a major international trading port. Historical evidence records connections between the city and Arab merchants. The researchers therefore suggest that maritime routes and the movement of merchants and craftsmen may have helped transmit brass-making knowledge to southern China.What does the discovery reveal about medieval metallurgy in ChinaThe findings add important evidence to the history of brass production in China. Local brass production is generally thought to have begun around the tenth century AD, but the Guangzhou crucibles provide direct evidence from the ninth-tenth centuries. The researchers argue that the discovery helps explain how a specialised metallurgical technique became established locally. It also shows why archaeological workshops can reveal details that written records alone cannot provide. The study does not claim that every element of brass technology came from one place or through one route. Instead, it highlights a possible connection between western technological traditions, maritime trade and local production in Guangzhou. The evidence adds an important piece to the history of metallurgy in East Asia.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: US funded the breakthrough, China built at scale: How robot dogs entered the new arms race
articles.summary: International News: China’s Unitree Robotics, one of the world’s leading makers of humanoid and quadruped robots, built some of its most successful robot dogs on technolo.
articles.body: China’s Unitree Robotics, one of the world’s leading makers of humanoid and quadruped robots, built some of its most successful robot dogs on technological breakthroughs developed through US military-funded research, according to researchers involved in the programme and a former US defence technology official.The case of Unitree highlights a growing challenge for the United States in the race for advanced military and dual-use technologies: American government-funded research is producing important breakthroughs, but Chinese companies are often proving more effective at turning similar technologies into affordable, mass-produced products.Unitree’s $1,600 Go2 robot, launched in 2023, helped the company rapidly expand its presence in the global quadruped robot market. The company sold more than 18,000 quadruped robots and 5,500 humanoid robots last year, according to company filings, and was valued at about $9 billion ahead of its stock market debut.The technology behind Unitree’s popular robot dogs can be traced in part to research funded by the US Army Research Laboratory (ARL), the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) and other military programmes, researchers and a former US defence technology official told Reuters.The Army-funded programme helped advance key technologies for quadruped robots, including the placement of motors in the legs rather than relying on heavy central gearboxes. The approach improved a robot’s ability to sense and respond to uneven terrain.Gavin Kenneally, a former University of Pennsylvania researcher involved in the programme, said the Army-funded work became “basically, the first Unitree robot that had any kind of scale."Ben Katz, who worked at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology’s Biomimetic Robotics Lab, said the dimensions of Unitree’s popular Go series were “to the millimeter” almost identical to Mini Cheetah, a robot he helped develop as part of a consortium of universities funded by US military programmes.Reuters said it was the first media outlet to detail the connections between Unitree’s designs and the US Army-funded research.How US military research reached ChinaThe US Army funded the Robotics Collaborative Technology Alliance (RCTA) from 2010 to 2020. The programme brought together researchers from government, academia and industry, including the University of Pennsylvania, MIT, Boston Dynamics and NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory.General Dynamics Land Systems, the Michigan-based defence company that manufactures Abrams M1 tanks, was the alliance’s leading commercial partner.The research built on earlier work funded by DARPA at MIT. In 2016, University of Pennsylvania researchers, including Kenneally, developed a design that eliminated heavy central gearboxes and instead placed motors directly in the robot’s legs.The change allowed the machines to respond more effectively to terrain and helped advance the development of agile quadruped robots.In 2019, MIT researchers unveiled the Mini Cheetah, which incorporated features developed at the University of Pennsylvania while adding greater strength and the ability to perform backflips.Katz had published his master's thesis months earlier, detailing the actuators used in Mini Cheetah. Within six months, he said, Chinese companies were manufacturing copies of the actuators that could be purchased online.Unitree founder Wang Xingxing had already established the company three years earlier. In his 2016 master's thesis at Shanghai University, which Reuters reviewed, Wang cited MIT's research on the Cheetah and earlier versions of the robot.Wang's thesis also referenced Kenneally's Army-funded research and acknowledged the US laboratory's "pioneering" contributions. He examined design changes aimed at speeding up development and said the findings could have future "defense, security, family and education" applications.Unitree says on its website that it “independently developed the motors, reducers, controllers, and even some sensors of the quadruped robot.”Katz said he decided not to commercialise his actuator design because he believed there was not a sufficient market. He said China's ability to manufacture such components quickly had helped advance robotics.Robotics “has advanced a lot because of the availability of actuators,” Katz said.Joao Ramos, who conducted research alongside Katz at MIT, said Unitree copied the Mini Cheetah's shape, structure and design. At the same time, he credited the Chinese company with engineering the technology for mass production.“The actual practical implementation, bringing it to real life, that's all on them,” Ramos said.China turned research into mass-market robotsThe Unitree story points to a wider difference between the US and Chinese approaches to advanced manufacturing.The United States has maintained a strong position in fundamental research and software, while China has built large industrial clusters capable of producing components at scale and at lower prices.Chinese manufacturers have used extensive supplier networks, component factories and access to critical minerals to expand rapidly in areas including robotics, drones, electric vehicles and solar panels.Unitree's base in Hangzhou is surrounded by suppliers producing motors, gears, actuators and other components used in robotics. China's dominance in the processing of critical minerals used in robotic magnets has also helped manufacturers reduce costs and accelerate production.Reyk Knuhtsen, a robotics analyst at SemiAnalysis, described the US failure to commercialise domestic research as a “dropped ball”. He said venture capital in the US has often favoured software businesses with higher returns rather than capital-intensive manufacturing.“This is a very big hill for the U.S. to climb,” he said.Jaret Riddick, a former director of the Army Research Laboratory who oversaw the robotics project, said the programme did help kick-start the US quadruped robotics industry. But without sufficient support for large-scale manufacturing, Unitree in China “just kind of consumed that space.”Unitree now faces US restrictionsThe US government has increasingly moved to restrict Chinese robotics technology on national security grounds.In June, the Pentagon added Unitree to a list of Chinese military companies, describing it as a “contributor to the Chinese defense industrial base.” The designation does not amount to a direct sanction but restricts the US military's future use of Unitree technology.In July, the Federal Communications Commission also banned imports of future models of foreign-made humanoid and quadruped robots, including those produced by Unitree. China has threatened retaliation against the FCC move.The Chinese embassy in Washington defended Chinese companies, saying they were making new technologies more affordable and accessible internationally. It accused the US of “market distortion and unilateral bullying.”US researchers who spoke to Reuters did not argue that government-funded research should have been kept secret. Instead, they said Washington needs to develop a stronger system for helping domestic companies move discoveries from laboratories into commercial manufacturing.ARL spokesperson Amanda Ligon said the research “strengthened the broader U.S. robotics ecosystem” and informed subsequent work across government and the private sector.ARL also said publication of the research was important for scientific and technological advancement.Vijay Kumar, dean at Penn Engineering, said the US remains strong in innovation and software development but needs greater access to capital, industrial capacity, skilled workers and component supply chains to scale new technologies.US military also used Chinese robot dogsThe gap between American research and manufacturing capacity has also created an unusual situation in which the US military has itself explored Chinese-made robot dogs.In September 2023, the US Army obtained a federal waiver from rules requiring government agencies to prioritise American-made products to purchase two Unitree Go2 robots, according to procurement records. The records described the robots as important because sufficient US-produced alternatives of “a satisfactory quality" were not available.Reuters could not establish whether the purchases were completed.The US military has also experimented with weaponising quadruped robots. In September 2023, US Marines conducted an exercise involving a Go1 robot fitted with a rocket launcher for remote firing.Chinese military exercises have similarly featured robot dogs. Chinese state television has shown Unitree Go2 robots operating alongside People's Liberation Army troops. Another modified Unitree B1 robot has been shown firing a mounted assault rifle.Unitree has maintained that its products are intended for civilian use. In 2022, the company joined US robotics firms in signing an open letter pledging not to weaponise robots, citing the risks of harm and serious ethical concerns.Walking robots are not yet widely deployed on battlefields, but both the US and China are examining their potential for military applications, including surveillance, reconnaissance and operations in difficult terrain.US defence robots remain far more expensiveAmerican companies continue to produce military-grade quadruped robots, but at substantially higher prices and smaller volumes.Kenneally's Ghost Robotics has supplied about 1,000 Vision 60 robots, mainly to military and government customers for surveillance and search operations in harsh environments. Its first customer was Navy Special Warfare Command, which oversees Navy SEAL teams.The Vision 60 sells for upwards of $165,000, while Unitree lists its B-series robot for less than $100,000 in the US.Ghost Robotics has also faced challenges in reducing its dependence on Chinese components. Some components of its robots are manufactured in China, although the company has been shifting its supply chain.The company moved its motor supply from China to South Korea two years ago but continues to face difficulties replacing Chinese magnets and certain metal components, according to Kenneally.In 2024, South Korean defence company LIG Defense & Aerospace acquired a 60% stake in Ghost Robotics for $240 million. The company is also exploring production in Taiwan.Kenneally said reducing dependence on Chinese manufacturing would require partnerships with countries that have the industrial capacity the US currently lacks.“We need to work closely with our allies,” he said. “There's absolutely no path forward without them.”China’s industrial strategy widens the gapChina's advantage in robotics is not limited to individual companies. It is linked to a broader industrial policy that has channelled capital into advanced manufacturing.In 2015, Chinese President Xi Jinping announced a 10-year strategy aimed at establishing Chinese leadership in industries including robotics, electric vehicles and green energy.Since then, Chinese companies have benefited from access to capital, dense manufacturing networks and suppliers capable of producing components at scale.The approach has allowed companies to tolerate lower margins while expanding production and market share.Kenneally said the competition therefore goes beyond individual robotics firms.“This isn't just a competition between U.S. and Chinese robotics companies,” he said. “It's between private U.S. companies and China’s coordinated national strategy.”For Washington, the challenge is now how to ensure that government-funded breakthroughs do not remain confined to research laboratories while companies in China turn similar technologies into cheaper products at scale.The Pentagon has declined to comment on Unitree's commercialisation of US Army-funded research. The White House did not respond to requests for comment on US industrial policy.The episode underlines a wider concern for US defence planners: maintaining an edge in military technology may depend not only on producing breakthrough research, but also on building the industrial capacity needed to manufacture those technologies quickly, cheaply and at scale.

articles.title: In 2020, a Brazilian mother and daughter began collecting discarded bottles; years later, more than 8,000 glass bottles had become the walls of their seven-bedroom home that glows during sunrise
articles.summary: When people go on a trip, they make sure to carry back a suitcase full of memories.
articles.body: When people go on a trip, they make sure to carry back a suitcase full of memories. From photos to souvenirs, they invest in numerous things to ensure that they have something to remember the good times by. But one thing they always end up forgetting is to carry back the waste and deposit it correctly in the dustbins. From bottles to food wrappers, numerous pieces of evidence of human adventure collect on beaches and in forests for years, until they are all you can see on the land.On the Brazilian island of Itamaraca, one house is making a simple question that is hard to ignore. The waste tourists leave behind on a beach can either accumulate on the sand for years, or become useful in the wall or roof of a home. This is a step Edna Dantas and her daughter Maria Gabreilly Dantas took.The mother-daughter duo created Casa de Sal (The Salt House), a seven-room dwelling with the help of recycled wood, pallets, toothpaste tubes, and yes, more than 8,000 glass bottles. The home is located in Pernambuco, where beaches, biodiversity, rising tourism, and discarded waste paint a contrasting but realistic picture.A beach problem, a home solutionDuring the problem, Edna observed the bottles piling up near the shore and decided to try something that sounded almost impossible. She wanted to build a home with glass bottles, not as decorations but as a part of the structure. The 55-year-old is a socio-environmental educator while her 27-year-old daughter works in sustainable fashion. It took them two years to collect all the materials and together, they turned a family habit of reuse into a construction project.For their home, they assembled the bottles into glass walls, recycled pallets for partitions and made the roofing from toothpaste tubes. The first finished room was about 215 square feet and served as a sewing workshop while the rest of the home slowly took shape.“The first year and a half was pure ingenuity: no conventional bathroom, washing dishes in a basin. But we never lost sight of our vision,” Maria told Diario AS.According to Good Good Good, the two have collected more than 13,000 bottles since the beginning of the project and used about 8,000 in their home. The result is bright not only for a sustainable future, but also in appearance. As the sunlight passes through the bottles, the house shines bright with its purpose, reminding visitors that beauty often comes from the most surprising of places.The project not only shone light on environmental conservation but also patriarchal notions. Maria said workers brought in for specific tasks often wanted to correct them and not just help them. “As if we lacked capacity,” she said. “People think that one day we found a magic bottle with a genie inside,” Maria told Black Enterprise. “They don’t realise this requires skill, management, vision. And being a woman in this environment is doubly hard.” Construction is still often treated as male territory, especially when the builders are women leading an unconventional project. That is why the phrase “it has our signature” matters.Why glass mattersGlass sounds clean since it can be recycled again and again. But that does not help much when bottles are abandoned in mangroves, streets and beaches, without reaching the factories where they can be recycled. It is heavy, easy to discard, and often unattractive for informal collectors when the return is low.“These bottles are not going to disappear. Without policies to regulate their production or penalise abandonment, the least we can do is find ways to reuse them,” Edna told Black Enterprise. “If you throw a bottle away and it doesn’t break, it’ll still be there in a year.” If bottles are sold in tourist towns, someone has to plan what happens after they have served their purpose. For coastal communities, this is not an abstract environmental issue. It is the broken glass near the sand, the trash after a crowded weekend, and the extra cleanup that often falls on residents.Moreover, Brazil's housing deficit was estimated at 5,773,983 homes in 2024, representing 7.4 per cent of occupied private households, according to the Ministry of Cities, citing data from Fundação João Pinheiro. That means Casa de Sal sits in the middle of two pressures at once. The country needs more decent housing, while local communities are also being asked to absorb the cost of waste. In a social media post, Edna shared an alarming statistic that claims it can take up to seven generations, 184 years, for Black women in Brazil to buy a house of their own. Edna cites “environmental racism” as the catalyst for this project, one she hopes can provide repair and healing for everyone in her community.Edna grew up in a family that reused materials out of necessity and passed down their innate creativity onto her. “My childhood was marked by creativity,” she told Globo. “I made my own bamboo toys, recycled whatever I could. We didn’t know it was environmental activism, it was just how we survived.”Indigenous to the Quilombola, an Afro-Brazilian people who are descendants of Africans who escaped slavery and started their own settlements in Brazil, the Dantas women see it as their responsibility to respect nature, with roots both in African and Indigenous cultures.Today, the Salt House is listed on Airbnb, while the duo also runs workshops to teach the local community about sustainable building. They have also launched an upcycled accessories brand, hand-sewing tote bags from found and reclaimed materials. For the Dantas women, the project continues to demonstrate how discarded materials can be transformed into useful and meaningful creations.What are your views on this? articles.title: ‘Sava’s Titanic,’ the century-old sunken shipwreck emerges as Europe’s rivers fall to record lows
articles.summary: Europe News: A century-old shipwreck has resurfaced from the Sava River in Serbia as an intense drought leaves waterways across Europe at exceptionally low levels..
articles.body: A century-old shipwreck has resurfaced from the Sava River in Serbia as an intense drought leaves waterways across Europe at exceptionally low levels. The rusting remains of the Slovenian, a steam tugboat built in 1913, emerged near the Serbian town of Sremska Mitrovica earlier in August, revealing far more of the vessel than locals have seen in years. Serbian media have nicknamed the wreck “Sava’s Titanic”, turning an environmental warning into an unexpected historical spectacle. Historian Andrija Popovic, head of the town museum, told CBS News that there had been considerable local interest because the wreck had not been this visible for several years. The ship's appearance is part of a much wider pattern across Europe, where falling river levels have exposed forgotten warships, ancient structures and even prehistoric animal remains. According to CBS News, the drought has also disrupted shipping, power generation, agriculture and water supplies, showing how dramatically prolonged heat and dryness are reshaping the continent's rivers. The exposed wreck therefore offers a striking reminder of how changing water levels can reveal traces of the past while signalling the growing pressures facing Europe’s waterways.Why was the emergence of a century-old shipwreck from the Sava River shockingThe wreck of the Slovenian surfaced earlier this month near Sremska Mitrovica, around 72 kilometres northwest of Belgrade. Although portions of the vessel have appeared above the water during previous periods of low river levels, its latest emergence is unusually extensive. The remains show the rusted hull of a vessel that once played a role in commercial and wartime transport along the Danube and its surrounding waterways. The ship was approximately 177 feet (54 metres) long and was originally named Vag, after the Vah River, the longest river in Slovakia. Built in Budapest in 1913, it was equipped with a steam engine and used to tow heavy cargo between Budapest and other settlements along the Danube. Speaking to CBS News, historian Andrija Popovic said the wreck had not been so exposed for several years. He described the appearance as something that people do not encounter every day, explaining the fascination surrounding the vessel now that the Sava has retreated so dramatically. The ship's history also helps explain why its emergence is more than a curious sight on a drying riverbed. The vessel survived two world wars before finally sinking in 1945, leaving a physical trace of Europe's turbulent twentieth-century history beneath the Sava.The ‘Sava’s Titanic’ survived two world wars before sinkingThe ship's story stretches back to the final years of the Austro-Hungarian Empire. After the First World War, the dissolution of the empire changed ownership of the vessel. According to Popovic, the ship became part of the newly formed Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes as part of war reparations and was renamed Slovenian. The vessel later found itself caught up in the Second World War. After Nazi Germany occupied Yugoslavia, the ship remained in the region. Following the liberation of Belgrade in 1944, Yugoslav anti-fascist forces used it to transport wounded fighters and equipment as they advanced westwards against German forces. Its final journey came in late April 1945, near the end of the war. The Slovenian was carrying wounded fighters when it struck a German mine. The explosion sank the vessel, which has remained in essentially the same location ever since. That wartime history has given the shipwreck an unusual significance for the local community. Its rusting remains are effectively a submerged historical record, preserving part of the story of the region's transport network and the final stages of the Second World War. Now, decades after it disappeared beneath the Sava, the changing river level is revealing that history to a new generation.Europe’s drying rivers are revealing warships, mammoth bones and ancient ruinsThe emergence of the Slovenian is not an isolated event. Across Europe, unusually low river levels are exposing objects and structures that have remained hidden underwater for decades, centuries or even longer. In Serbia, the shrinking Danube has revealed the remains of German ships from the Second World War near the country's border with Romania. The vessels belonged to Nazi Germany's Black Sea fleet and were deliberately sunk as German forces retreated from Romania towards the end of the war. Some of the wrecks still contain weapons, creating additional hazards for people exploring the exposed riverbed. Other discoveries have appeared elsewhere. In Italy, severe drought has exposed sections of an ancient bridge over the Tiber River that was once used by Roman emperors. In Bulgaria, receding Danube waters allowed researchers to discover and recover a collection of woolly mammoth bones, including a jawbone, tusks, shoulder blade and ribs. The concentration of the remains suggested that the bones belonged to the same young animal. But beneath the fascination of these discoveries lies a much more serious environmental story.The Danube had reached record-low levels, severely affecting nuclear power plants in Hungary and Romania and halting traffic along parts of Europe's second-largest waterway. The prolonged drought has also damaged crops from the Netherlands to Bosnia and contributed to water shortages extending towards the Alps. According to the European Drought Observatory, around half of the European Union and the United Kingdom were experiencing drought conditions by late July 2026, with 9% of the territory at the most severe “alert” level. Europe is also the world's fastest-warming continent, with temperatures rising at roughly twice the global average since the 1980s, according to the EU's Copernicus Climate Change Service. Serbian hydrology expert Dejan Vladikovic also told CBS News that the current drought resulted from a combination of limited winter snowfall and an exceptionally dry spring. He warned that similar conditions could become more frequent, describing a future in which such periods may become “a new normalcy”. The Slovenian may therefore look like an archaeological curiosity emerging from the Sava, but its appearance is also a visible measure of just how far Europe's rivers have fallen. The lower the water drops, the more of the continent's hidden past becomes visible, while the disruption to transport, agriculture, electricity and water supplies reveals the present-day cost of a hotter and drier climate.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 6 Indians on board hijacked cargo ship carrying Turkish weapons off Somalia's coast
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Six Indians were among the 10-member crew of a Cameroon-flagged cargo ship hijacked by pirates off Somalia’s Puntland coast earlier this week, news ag.
articles.body: Six Indians were among the 10-member crew of a Cameroon-flagged cargo ship hijacked by pirates off Somalia’s Puntland coast earlier this week, news agency AP reported citing a Somali official on Thursday.The M/V LUTUF was seized on Monday about 3.5 nautical miles off Marraya in Puntland’s Eyl district and was later taken towards the Nugaal coast, the official said.The vessel, owned by Polar Movement Shipping, was carrying Turkish weapons bound for a military training facility in Mogadishu, along with communications and satellite equipment. Its crew comprised six Indian nationals, one Turkish national, one Georgian and two Serbian security guards.The official said eight pirates were believed to have seized the vessel. They were allegedly linked to a group previously involved in the hijacking of the M/V Sward on April 26.Two Turkish-owned vessels later approached the hijacked ship, while Turkish helicopters and drones monitored the area, the official said. A small boat carrying two men also approached the vessel on Tuesday and delivered khat, a stimulant commonly chewed in Somalia.The official said an airstrike followed after the boat returned to shore, killing four men and injuring two others. The circumstances of the strike, including who carried it out and whether those killed were involved in the hijacking, could not be independently verified by the news agency.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A strange wooden log found beneath Zambia’s Kalambo Falls was dismissed for decades, then archaeologists dated it to 476,000 years ago
articles.summary: Rest of World News: For decades, a strangely shaped log buried beneath Zambia’s Kalambo Falls sat at the edge of an archaeological mystery. When archaeologist J. Desmond .
articles.body: For decades, a strangely shaped log buried beneath Zambia’s Kalambo Falls sat at the edge of an archaeological mystery. When archaeologist J. Desmond Clark uncovered it in the 1950s, the timber had tapered ends and a deliberate-looking notch cut into its surface, suggesting that someone had shaped it rather than leaving it to the river. But Clark had no reliable way to establish how far back it belonged. Radiocarbon dating could not reach remotely far enough, while an early uranium-series estimate produced an uncertain age. More than half a century later, archaeologists returned to the site and found additional pieces of timber with matching cut marks.This time, luminescence dating of the surrounding sand provided an answer: the wooden structure was at least 476,000 years old. It is among the earliest known evidence of people deliberately shaping and joining wood, offering a rare glimpse of technology that almost never survives in the archaeological record. The discovery is especially important because wood normally decays long before archaeological researchers can study it. Its preservation at Kalambo Falls was made possible by waterlogged conditions, allowing scientists to examine evidence of woodworking that would otherwise have disappeared without leaving a trace.A wooden clue that refused to fit the recordClark was working at a site beneath Kalambo Falls, a 235-metre waterfall on the Kalambo River. The excavation was producing the sort of evidence expected from a Palaeolithic occupation: stone artefacts, animal bones and traces of activity from a distant human past.Then there was the timber. The log had been narrowed towards its ends and carried a carefully made notch. Its shape did not fit comfortably with the idea of a branch simply being altered by flowing water. Clark believed that somebody had worked it, probably using stone tools. Yet archaeology in the 1950s had a serious problem when it came to material this old. Recognising an artefact was one thing. Establishing its age was quite another.As reported, radiocarbon dating was of little use. Its practical range stopped at roughly 50,000 years, far short of what the Kalambo material appeared to represent. The result from Clark’s sample effectively said that it was beyond the method’s limit.A uranium-series attempt produced a figure of around 180,000 years. It was an intriguing number, but not one that could settle the matter. The evidence was too uncertain, and Clark never got the chance to see the question resolved. For decades, the timber remained an archaeological puzzle, waiting for newer dating techniques capable of testing its extraordinary age more precisely.The second excavation brought Clark’s mystery back to lifeDecades later, archaeologists returned to the same area as part of the Deep Roots of Humanity project. The work, led by Larry Barham of the University of Liverpool, brought modern excavation and dating techniques to a site that had already challenged an earlier generation of archaeologists. The new excavation produced something particularly useful: more wood.Several pieces lay in overlapping positions, and some carried notches that corresponded with the shape and arrangement of the timber around them. The resemblance to Clark’s earlier find made the old discovery much harder to dismiss as an isolated piece of unusually shaped wood.There was also evidence on the surfaces themselves. Scraped areas and marks resembling those produced by adze-like tools appeared around the notch, while the adjoining timber carried V-shaped cuts. Taken together, the marks suggested that people had deliberately altered the wood and fitted one piece against another.The question that had stopped Clark was now ready for a different kind of answer.The age came from the sand, not the timberThe team did not need to date the wood directly. Instead, the researchers turned to the sediment in which it had been buried.The method is known as luminescence dating. It works on mineral grains, such as those found in sand. While exposed at the surface, these grains are reset by sunlight. Once they become buried, small amounts of natural radiation accumulate within them. Measuring that stored signal can provide an estimate of how long the grains have been away from daylight.The study published in Nature, titled ‘Evidence for the earliest structural use of wood at least 476,000 years ago’ revealed that at Kalambo Falls, the surrounding sediment produced an age of at least 476,000 years, with an uncertainty of about 23,000 years.That result placed the wooden structure far beyond the limits of the dating techniques available when Clark excavated the site. It also made the old uranium-series estimate look dramatically too young.The timber was not simply ancient. It belonged to a period almost half a million years ago.What the builders actually made remains uncertainThe excavated pieces show that two sections of wood were shaped and joined. That is significant, but it does not reveal the complete form of whatever once stood there. There is no surviving roof, wall system or complete floor that would justify confidently describing it as a house.The researchers have instead suggested several possible uses. The joined timber could have formed part of a platform or walkway. It might have provided a raised surface for keeping objects away from wet ground. It could also have been associated with a larger structure whose other components were made from materials that did not survive. The distinction matters. Archaeology often works with fragments, and a fragment can demonstrate a technique without revealing the whole object.What can be said with much greater confidence is that the wood was selected and modified intentionally. Someone had to choose timber suitable for the job, cut it, shape it and make the pieces work together.Why the wood survived when so much else disappearedThe same river environment that helped people use the landscape also helped preserve evidence of what they did there.The timber had been buried in permanently waterlogged sediment, where oxygen levels were low. Decay is slowed under such conditions, allowing organic material to survive for periods that would be almost impossible in a dry, exposed archaeological site.It creates a strange imbalance in the record of early human technology. Archaeologists may see thousands of stone artefacts from a particular period and assume that stone tells most of the story. In reality, it may simply be the part of the story that survived.Wood could have been used extensively for handles, platforms, shelters, containers, traps, tools and other everyday objects. Most traces would have disappeared.Kalambo offers a rare glimpse of that missing material world.The people who made it are not identifiedThe age of the structure is clear enough to place it deep in the Middle Pleistocene, but the excavation does not identify the hominin species responsible for the construction.The researchers have been careful on this point. The evidence does not provide a secure species attribution, and the paper does not attempt to attach the structure to a particular hominin group.That restraint is important because human evolution was not a simple sequence in which one species neatly replaced another. Several hominin populations existed across Africa during the period in question, and the archaeological record is often too incomplete to connect a particular artefact with a particular species.What the Kalambo material does provide is behavioural evidence. Whoever made the structure was capable of selecting wood for a purpose, altering its shape with tools and joining separate pieces. Those actions required more than simply picking up a naturally useful branch.Clark had seen the same evidence, but not its ageClark's original interpretation was not necessarily wrong because his dating was wrong. He had recognised deliberate shaping in the timber, but the technology available to him could not establish when that work had happened.The modern excavation did not transform a natural log into an artefact. It supplied a stronger archaeological context and a dating method capable of reaching far deeper into the past.In that sense, the most important change took place outside the riverbed. The evidence had been waiting there for decades.The discovery also shows how much archaeological interpretation can depend on preservation. A wooden structure from nearly half a million years ago would normally be almost impossible to find. At Kalambo, the river kept it sealed in the mud.There are no surviving written records from this period, no buildings standing above the ground and no complete account of what the structure was for. There is simply shaped timber, tool marks, sediment and the traces left by people who lived in a very different landscape.And that distinction is perhaps the most revealing part of the Kalambo discovery. The oldest known wooden structure is not a neatly preserved ancient building waiting to tell its story. It is a small, damaged piece of evidence from a much larger world that has mostly disappeared.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Two Belgian climbers vanished in the Alps in 1992; melting ice has finally revealed their remains 34 years later
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Two Belgian mountaineers who disappeared in the Swiss Alps in 1992 have finally been identified after their remains emerged from a retreating glacier .
articles.body: Two Belgian mountaineers who disappeared in the Swiss Alps in 1992 have finally been identified after their remains emerged from a retreating glacier 34 years later. The men, who were 39 and 41 when they vanished, had set out in the Weissmies region but never reached their planned destination. Despite searches at the time, only a backpack was recovered and the pair remained missing for more than three decades. On July 26, 2026, a hiker discovered two bodies on the Trift Glacier near Saas-Grund in Switzerland's Valais canton. The remains were taken for forensic examination, where DNA testing formally confirmed their identities, bringing an end to a decades-old mystery while highlighting how retreating Alpine glaciers are exposing long-hidden remains.Belgian climbers disappeared in Alps during mountain tripThe two Belgian men disappeared in September 1992 while travelling through the Weissmies region of the Swiss Alps. They had set out from the Weissmies Hut at an altitude of about 2,726 metres and were planning to reach the Almageller Hut. Their intended route involved crossing the 4,017-metre Weissmies, one of the major peaks in the region. According to reports from the time and subsequent accounts, the men encountered extremely poor weather conditions. They never arrived at their planned destination, triggering searches in the surrounding mountains. Rescue teams eventually recovered a mountaineering backpack, but there was no sign of the two men. Their disappearance remained unresolved for 34 years.The breakthrough came on July 26, 2026, when a hiker reported finding two bodies on the Trift Glacier near Saas-Grund in the canton of Valais. The area lies in southern Switzerland, relatively close to the Italian border and within the broader Alpine region where the men had disappeared. The remains were recovered and transferred to the Institute of Forensic Medicine at Valais Hospital in Sion. Authorities began working to establish who the bodies belonged to, with the age of the remains and their location raising the possibility that they could be connected to one of the region's long-standing missing-person cases.DNA testing finally identified the menThe identification was eventually confirmed through DNA analysis. Valais police said a direct comparison of DNA profiles formally established that the remains belonged to the two mountaineers who had gone missing in the Weissmies region in 1992. The DNA confirmation is significant because it removes the uncertainty that can surround the identification of remains recovered from glaciers. The discovery therefore did not merely provide a possible lead in the decades-old case. It formally established the identities of the two missing Belgian men and brought their long-running disappearance to a close.Their exact cause of death remains unclearAlthough the discovery has solved the question of who the remains belonged to, it has not necessarily answered what happened to the men in 1992. Authorities have not publicly established the exact circumstances or cause of their deaths. The men were last known to be travelling through mountainous terrain in difficult weather conditions. Their planned journey involved high-altitude terrain, where snow, ice, poor visibility and rapidly changing weather can create serious risks. However, there is no confirmed public evidence establishing whether they died after a fall, an accident, exposure or another specific event. It would therefore be speculative to claim that they fell into a crevasse or were killed by an avalanche unless investigators provide further evidence.Retreating glaciers are exposing long-hidden remainsThe discovery also illustrates a phenomenon increasingly being seen across the Alps. As glaciers retreat, material that has remained buried beneath ice for decades can become exposed. In some cases, that material includes the remains of people who disappeared during mountain expeditions many years earlier. Valais police have noted that the retreat of glaciers repeatedly reveals the remains of people who disappeared in the mountains decades ago. The latest discovery is therefore part of a wider pattern rather than an isolated incident.The broader scientific picture makes such discoveries increasingly possible. Switzerland's glaciers have experienced significant ice loss in recent decades, with the rate of retreat accelerating. According to Swiss glacier monitoring data, the country's glaciers lost about 24% of their ice volume between 2015 and 2025. The loss was considerably greater than in the preceding decades, showing the increasing pace of glacier retreat.In 2025 alone, Switzerland lost around 3% of its remaining glacier volume, equivalent to roughly 1.4 cubic kilometres of ice. Continued warming and repeated periods of unusually high temperatures have contributed to increasingly rapid melting.Other missing climbers have also been foundThe Belgian climbers are not the first people to be recovered after disappearing in the Swiss Alps. In recent years, retreating glaciers have exposed remains connected to several long-standing missing-person cases.In 2025, the remains of a Swiss mountaineer who disappeared in 1994 were found on a glacier on the Ober Gabelhorn in Valais. In another case, the remains of a German mountaineer who disappeared in 1990 were discovered on the Stockjigletscher near Zermatt and later identified.One of the most striking cases occurred in 2017, when a shrinking glacier in Switzerland revealed the remains of Marcelin and Francine Dumoulin, a couple who disappeared in 1942. Their discovery came 75 years after they were last seen.Glaciers can preserve remains for decadesA glacier can conceal people and objects beneath layers of ice for extraordinarily long periods. Extremely cold conditions can slow decomposition, while the surrounding ice can effectively hide remains from search teams and prevent them from being visible at the surface. Glaciers are also dynamic environments. Ice moves slowly downhill, meaning that material trapped within a glacier can potentially shift over time before eventually becoming exposed as the ice melts. This means the location where remains emerge does not necessarily represent the precise place where a person originally disappeared. In the case of the two Belgian mountaineers, authorities have confirmed their identities but have not publicly reconstructed every stage of what happened to them after they disappeared.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Detroit school students can earn $100 every week just by attending all their classes as district schools bring back cash rewards for perfect attendance
articles.summary: US News: Detroit Public Schools Community District is bringing back its \"Perfect Attendance Pays\" programme for the 2026-27 school year, giving high-school stu.
articles.body: Detroit Public Schools Community District is bringing back its "Perfect Attendance Pays" programme for the 2026-27 school year, giving high-school students a chance to earn $100 for each qualifying period of perfect attendance. The programme is also being expanded to students in grades 6-8, who can receive $50 for a qualifying period. The initiative comes as Detroit continues to grapple with high levels of chronic absenteeism and is part of a wider effort to encourage students to attend school regularly. During the previous programme, about 12,800 high-school students received at least one $100 Visa gift card. The district is now extending the incentive to younger students while also investing in transportation, attendance staff and other support aimed at getting more students into classrooms consistently.Detroit school students earned up to $1,000 for perfect attendanceThe programme rewards students who maintain perfect attendance during designated five-day qualifying cycles. Under the previous programme, eligible high-school students had to attend all their scheduled classes throughout the cycle to receive a $100 Visa gift card. The programme ran from January 5 through March 20, 2026, with 10 qualifying cycles, allowing students who met the requirement every time to earn up to $1,000.The structure is designed to reward consistent attendance rather than occasional appearances. Students who failed to maintain perfect attendance during one cycle could still qualify during a later cycle, giving them another opportunity to earn the incentive.The previous programme reached a substantial share of Detroit's district high-school population. About 12,800 students received at least one $100 Visa gift card during the 2025-26 programme, according to figures reported by Chalkbeat Detroit. DPSCD had about 15,247 students across 26 high schools at the time, meaning roughly 84% received at least one reward. The number includes students who qualified for a single cycle as well as those who earned rewards during multiple cycles.Middle-school students are joining the programmeFor 2026-27, DPSCD is expanding the incentive beyond high school. Students in grades 6-8 can now qualify for $50 for a qualifying period of perfect attendance, while high-school students remain eligible for the $100 reward. The expansion brings the programme to students earlier in their school careers, giving the district another way to encourage regular attendance before absenteeism becomes a longer-term problem. The initiative is included among the district's attendance priorities in its adopted $1.1 billion budget for 2026-27.Detroit continues to face an attendance crisisThe programme comes against a backdrop of widespread absenteeism across the district. About 60.9% of DPSCD students were chronically absent during the 2024-25 school year, according to figures reported by Michigan Public. Chronic absenteeism generally means missing at least 10% of the school year. For a large urban school district such as Detroit, prolonged absences can mean students lose substantial amounts of classroom instruction and can fall further behind academically. DPSCD has therefore made attendance a central part of its broader school improvement strategy, combining financial incentives with transportation assistance, attendance personnel and other services.High-school absenteeism has shown improvementThe district has reported a notable improvement in high-school attendance since its attendance efforts intensified. High-school chronic absenteeism fell from 64% in 2023-24 to 54% by the end of April 2026, according to figures cited in recent reporting. The change came during a period when DPSCD was using several approaches to address attendance, including the Perfect Attendance Pays programme. The gift-card incentive is, therefore one element of a wider push to bring more students into classrooms and keep them there consistently.Millions are being invested in attendanceDPSCD's $1.1 billion 2026-27 budget includes $13.9 million for efforts to reduce chronic absenteeism. The allocation supports a range of measures rather than being limited to student rewards. The funding covers initiatives including attendance agents, financial incentives for middle- and high-school students, wraparound services and yellow-school-bus service pilots. The district is effectively treating attendance as a problem that requires both motivation and practical support.Transportation is another focusGetting students to school can itself be a challenge, particularly for families who rely on public transportation. As part of its attendance strategy, DPSCD is expanding yellow-school-bus service to Pershing High School and Cody High School during the 2026-27 school year. The district's transportation measures are intended to address some of the practical barriers that can keep students away from school. Financial rewards may encourage attendance, but reliable ways to get to the classroom are also important for students who face transportation difficulties.The programme is part of a wider attendance strategyDPSCD's "Perfect Attendance Pays" initiative is designed around a simple idea: give students an immediate reward for maintaining a behaviour that can have long-term academic benefits. Rather than waiting until a student becomes severely absent, the district is using regular incentives to encourage students to keep attending. The approach also fits into the district's broader Blueprint 2027 goals, which include improving attendance and reducing chronic absenteeism. The financial incentive is being used alongside other interventions rather than as a standalone solution.Not every chronically absent student can benefitThe programme has also highlighted the difficulty of reaching students with the most serious attendance problems. Superintendent Nikolai Vitti has acknowledged that the incentive has not yet reached some students with severe absenteeism, including those who miss dozens of school days. That creates a natural limit to a perfect-attendance reward. Students who are already able to attend regularly may find it easier to qualify, while those facing major barriers such as transportation problems, family circumstances or other challenges may struggle to meet the requirement. For those students, DPSCD's additional attendance services and support programmes become particularly important.Detroit is expanding the experimentThe 2026-27 school year marks another step in Detroit's attempt to tackle chronic absenteeism through a combination of incentives and support. High-school students can continue to earn $100 Visa gift cards for qualifying periods of perfect attendance, while students in grades 6-8 are being brought into the programme at $50. The previous programme showed that the incentive could reach thousands of students, with about 12,800 high-schoolers receiving at least one reward. As DPSCD expands the programme, the district is betting that financial incentives, better transportation and additional student support can help turn more regular attendance into a lasting habit.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 16-year-old ran onto a Tennessee middle-school football field during a scuffle and tackled a player; school district banned her from its properties for life
articles.summary: US News: A 16-year-old girl in Tennessee has been charged after  she ran onto a football field during a middle school game and tackled a player. The incident h.
articles.body: A 16-year-old girl in Tennessee has been charged after she ran onto a football field during a middle school game and tackled a player. The incident happened on Tuesday night during a game between South Middle School and Cornersville Middle School at Franklin County High School in Winchester.The incident happened after South Middle School scored a touchdown and an extra point, authorities said, New York Post reported. A scuffle then broke out between two players at the end of the play. The 16-year-old girl ran onto the field after seeing the scuffle and tackled the South Middle School player involved in it.Video of the incident showed the girl running towards the player and taking him to the ground. The game was then brought to an early end as officials cleared the field and school resource officers dealt with the situation.According to the Franklin County Sheriff’s Office, a school resource officer met the girl as she left the field. She was then released to her parents, who were present at the game. The sheriff’s office charged the 16-year-old with assault and disorderly conduct.What happened on fieldThe incident was captured on video. The footage showed the teenager tackling the middle school player during the game. Another person, who appeared to be a coach, moved towards the pair after the player was taken to the ground.According to News Channel 5, the girl has been identified as Addison Hunnicutt. She reportedly told authorities that she ran onto the field because she was trying to protect her younger brother.Addison said she did not intend to target the other player without reason. “I wasn't going after this kid just to go after him,” she said. “That wasn't my intention at all.”She said she decided to step in after seeing what was happening on the field and feeling that no one was stopping it. “Seeing what they were doing to him and no one stopping it, that kind of made me the last choice. Somebody has to stop this,” Addison said.Her mother, Elizabeth Chumbley, was also in the stands watching the game. She said, "I'm seeing my son on the ground being attacked," Elizabeth said. "This wasn't just a football play. This is him on the ground being physically attacked by this other player."Addison’s attorney, David McKenzie, said the charges were excessive and argued that the events leading up to the incident should also be considered. “It’s not just a one-minute clip. It’s about the other 20 minutes of this game, what was going on this field, which prompted an otherwise fantastic little girl from a great family to enter the field,” McKenzie said.The father of the 13-year-old player who was tackled by Addison also spoke out publicly. In a Facebook post, he said his son did not deserve what happened and reminded people that a real child and family are behind the viral video. He also condemned the hateful and racial comments posted online.Girl faces lifetime ban The charges were followed by separate action from local school and sports authorities. Franklin County Schools banned the teenager from all district properties for life.The Tennessee Secondary School Athletic Association also imposed a ban on the girl. She will not be allowed to attend Cornersville Middle School home or away athletic events for one year.The school district's decision means the teenager is barred from entering its properties, while the athletic association's ban specifically covers Cornersville Middle School's athletic events.The principal of South Middle School praised school staff, coaches and school resource officers for their response to the incident. The school also said it plans to introduce additional security measures at future games.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 1932, Texas ranchers introduced axis deer from India for fenced hunting; the deer later escaped and spread across the Edwards Plateau
articles.summary: US News: Discover the impact of the invasive axis deer in Texas, their rapid population growth, and the ecological challenges they pose to native wildlife. Learn about their history, biological characteristics, and the ongoing management crisis stemming from their initial introduction in 1932.
articles.body: In 1932, Texas landowners introduced axis deer from the Indian subcontinent into the state and initially kept the animals behind high fences as a new hunting attraction. However, nearly a century after their initial release, the animals have outgrown their borders, thus transforming a localised introduction into a dominant wildlife population across most of the Texas Hill Country. According to data monitored by the Exotic Wildlife Association, thestatewide population of both managed and free-roaming axis deer has expanded significantly from historical baselines, reaching an estimated total of up to 125,000 animals.Moving out of fenced ranches to the Edwards PlateauThe original ambition behind the introduction was part of a broader Texas tradition of bringing non-native game animals onto private properties. Texas Parks & Wildlife records identify 1932 as the year axis deer were first released in the state by Richard Friedrich on the Bear Creek Ranch in Kerr County. The initial breeding pairs were sourced alongside other exotic wildlife through coastal ports and zoological supply networks, and some were sent to the San Antonio Zoo. The deer were attractive candidates for private ranches because they were well suited to the Hill Country’s mixture of open grassland, brush and wooded areas. Axis deer, also known as chital, are native to India and have a reddish-brown coat marked with white spots that they retain throughout their adult life.For decades, private ranches continued to stock exotic animals behind high fences; however, fences did not always manage to contain them. The Texas Parks & Wildlife notes that axis deer and other introduced ungulates were either released deliberately or escaped their confinement and eventually became established across major parts of Kerr, Bandera, Edwards and Real counties. Notably, in accordance with the Texas State Historical Association, the largest concentration of this species developed in the Edwards Plateau. Agencies now study these animals partly because of their potential competition with native wildlife and their impact on rangeland.A deer population that behaves differentlyAxis deer have several biological characteristics that shed light on their success rate in Texas. Researchers claim that the animals are primarily grazers, feeding heavily on grasses but also consuming forbs, sedges and woody browse. The species is generally found in herds ranging from a few animals to more than 100 and can reproduce during most of the year. In Texas, while most fawns are born between January and April, births can occur in other seasons as well. These flexible feeding habits can, however, bring them into competition with native white-tailed deer.A study published in the Journal of Fish and Wildlife Management found that free-ranging axis deer had expanded substantially across the Edwards Plateau. The historical survey data indicates that by 1994, Texas hosted an estimated 23,000 free-ranging axis deer, alongside 29,000 individuals maintained on high-fence ranches. This historical baseline footprint has expanded dramatically over the last three decades. Escaping containment at a steady rate, the species grew to heavily saturate its primary regional strongholds and spill into adjacent territories.The ecological concern is not just the number of animals, as several studies have cited that axis deer can consume substantially more forage than an individual native white-tailed deer, thus potentially increasing pressure on vegetation when populations become dense. Researchers have issued warnings that large axis populations can reduce the availability and hamper the quality of forage and may also affect agricultural land, especially in areas where livestock and wildlife depend on the same vegetation.Furthermore, a 2025 Texas A&M AgriLife Extension circular names chital deer among the most abundant and widespread exotic species in the state. While these animals remain managed on many enclosed estates, free-ranging populations now occur throughout the Edwards Plateau and northern South Texas Plains. This geographic spread has created a profound split-status framework: inside a high-fence perimeter, the deer is legally classified as private property and a lucrative commercial asset; the moment it escapes onto open range, it becomes an unregulated invasive threat. Texas addresses this paradox by delegating the ecological burden to the private sector, thus imposing no state bag limits or closed seasons on open range to incentivize year-round culling. Because the state classifies the species as invasive, unconfined axis deer have no state protection. However, this lack of biological protection does not exempt hunters from state authority, as Texas tightly enforces standard hunting licenses to maintain sovereign oversight over public safety corridors and the use of weapons, while landowner permissions protect private property boundaries during open-range culling operations.Therefore, what began as a managed population on an enclosed Kerr County estate has transformed into a permanent, highly aggressive management crisis across the central and southern plains. The animals’ flexible foraging habits, year-round reproduction, and rapid adaptation mean that their presence on the open range requires a permanent, highly vigilant containment and culling strategy rather than passive acceptance into the native ecosystem.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Pet owners dumped unwanted turtles in an Oregon park: A 2015 count found 30 of 50 basking turtles were invaders crowding out both native species
articles.summary: US News: In 2015, a count of turtles basking at Minto-Brown Island Park in Salem, Oregon, showed how a common pet could become a problem for native wildlife. O.
articles.body: In 2015, a count of turtles basking at Minto-Brown Island Park in Salem, Oregon, showed how a common pet could become a problem for native wildlife. Of 50 turtles observed at basking sites, 30 were non-native red-eared sliders, according to reporting by the Statesman Journal. The sliders were believed to have been released after being kept as pets. Once in the ponds and sloughs of the 1,200-acre park, they joined two native freshwater turtle species: the western painted turtle and the northwestern pond turtle. Both native species are considered species of conservation concern in Oregon. Basking sites are an important resource for turtles, since they use sunny logs, rocks, and other surfaces to warm their bodies. When non-native turtles occupy those sites in large numbers, native species may have fewer opportunities to use them.How pet turtles became a wildlife problemRed-eared sliders are among the most commonly kept pet turtles in the United States, but Oregon wildlife officials warn that releasing unwanted turtles outdoors is not a harmless alternative to keeping them in captivity. The Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife says the state has two native freshwater turtle species, the western painted turtle and the northwestern pond turtle. Both have low or declining populations. The agency identifies non-native red-eared sliders as a concern because they compete with native turtles for resources and can introduce diseases. Pet turtles should not be released into the wild. The problem is not limited to Oregon, since red-eared sliders have introduced populations in wetlands around the world. Their ability to survive in a range of freshwater habitats has made releases from the pet trade a persistent conservation issue.At Minto-Brown Island Park, the concern was visible on the basking structures themselves. A visitor could see several turtles sharing a log, but the species were not necessarily equal members of the local ecosystem. The red-eared slider is not native to Oregon, while the western painted turtle and northwestern pond turtle are.Oregon's State Wildlife Action Plan describes both native species as vulnerable to several pressures, including habitat loss, road mortality, predation and competition from invasive turtles. For the western painted turtle, the state specifically lists the release of pet turtles, including red-eared sliders, as a threat because introduced animals may outcompete native species for habitat.Competition is more complicated than a head countThe presence of more sliders than native turtles at a basking site does not, by itself, prove that every native turtle has been pushed aside, and that distinction matters. Scientists have had to test whether red-eared sliders actually affect native turtles under field conditions. A field experiment published in PeerJ examined an introduced red-eared slider population alongside western pond turtles, a native species of conservation concern. Researchers removed most of the sliders and monitored changes afterward. They found that the native turtles' body condition improved after the removal, although the researchers said the results were consistent with either direct or indirect competition. The study described this as the first evidence that introduced red-eared sliders can compete with a native turtle in the wild.Red-eared sliders can compete for food, nesting areas, basking sites and cover. Oregon officials also warn that non-native turtles may transmit parasites and diseases to native populations. The northwestern pond turtle and western painted turtle require suitable freshwater habitat, but they also need places outside the water for nesting and surfaces exposed to the sun for basking. Those requirements make urban parks with ponds and wetlands useful habitat, but only if the habitat remains available to native wildlife.The problem did not end with the 2015 countThe turtle issue at Minto-Brown Island Park continued to draw attention after the earlier survey, and researchers and conservation groups have worked on monitoring native and non-native turtles and improving basking habitat within the park. More recent observations have also examined another pressure: recreation. A preliminary study conducted in the park during the summer of 2022 recorded more than 500 hours of observations, and researchers counted over 2,100 park visitors and 305 turtles. Native turtles were more likely than red-eared sliders to react to nearby recreation by stopping their basking behavior and entering the water.That later research adds another factor to the management of an urban park where native turtles already face competition from an introduced species. The 2015 observation remains a simple illustration of the larger issue: thirty of the 50 basking turtles counted were invaders. For Oregon wildlife managers, the response is equally straightforward: unwanted pet turtles should not be released into ponds, rivers or parks. The state's native turtles already face declining populations and habitat pressures, and an animal released from someone's home can become one more competitor in the wild.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: O feriado 20 de novembro, Dia da Consciência Negra, cai em uma sexta-feira em 2026 e garante descanso prolongado nacional em homenagem a Zumbi dos Palmares.
articles.body:

O próximo feriado nacional acontece em 20 de novembro, quando é celebrado o Dia Nacional de Zumbi e da Consciência Negra. A data cairá em uma sexta-feira , formando três dias seguidos de descanso para quem não trabalha aos fins de semana.

Ela marca a morte de Zumbi dos Palmares, líder do Quilombo dos Palmares, no século XVII. Também é um momento de conscientização sobre a cultura negra e de reflexão sobre a luta contra o racismo e pela garantia dos direitos da população negra no Brasil.

Quem tem direito à folga no Dia da Consciência Negra?

Vale lembrar que nem todos os trabalhadores têm direito à folga nos feriados. A legislação permite o funcionamento de atividades consideradas essenciais e de outras categorias autorizadas a trabalhar nessas datas.

⚠️ Nesses casos, quem trabalha no feriado pode ter direito a remuneração em dobro ou a uma folga compensatória , conforme a legislação aplicável e as regras previstas em acordos ou convenções coletivas.

Ao todo, 2026 tem dez feriados nacionais, dos quais nove cairão em dias úteis .

Depois do Dia da Consciência Negra, em 20 de novembro, restará apenas o Natal, celebrado em 25 de dezembro, uma sexta-feira . A data forma três dias seguidos de descanso para quem não trabalha aos fins de semana.

Já as vésperas de Natal (24) e de Ano-Novo (31) serão pontos facultativos para os órgãos e entidades abrangidos pelo calendário oficial do governo federal . No setor privado, a concessão de folga nessas datas não é automática.

articles.body:
Dias depois de Jensen Huang deixar o comando da Nvidia , empresários, investidores e funcionários da fabricante de chips começaram a se mobilizar para tentar trazê-lo de volta.

➡️ A mobilização envolve diferentes iniciativas. Uma delas é uma carta aberta dirigida ao conselho de administração da Nvidia , que pede o retorno de Huang enquanto uma investigação independente esclarece os fatos.

A carta, chamada "Stand with Jensen" (Apoie Jensen), foi criada em 13 de novembro, um dia após o anúncio da saída de Huang.

Até a manhã desta segunda-feira (16), a página reunia mais de 170 mil assinaturas . A participação é aberta ao público.

Petição de apoio a Huang — Foto: Reprodução

Musk e outros nomes conhecidos apoiam a volta

Elon Musk declarou publicamente que apoiaria uma petição pela recondução de Huang. Em uma publicação na rede social X, escreveu: "Uma petição está em andamento para reconduzir Jensen, e eu também vou assiná-la".

Outros nomes conhecidos do setor aparecem entre os apoiadores da mobilização. É o caso de Tim Sweeney, fundador e presidente-executivo da Epic Games , empresa responsável pelo jogo Fortnite; Garry Tan , presidente da aceleradora de startups Y Combinator; e Travis Kalanick , cofundador do Uber.

O fundador da Replit, Amjad Masad, também ajudou a campanha. A empresa desenvolve uma plataforma que permite criar aplicativos e sites com auxílio de inteligência artificial. Segundo o jornal americano "The Wall Street Journal", Masad ajudou a corrigir problemas técnicos no site criado para receber assinaturas da carta aberta.

➡️ Os nomes e cargos profissionais atribuídos aos apoiadores na página da campanha não foram verificados de forma independente. Funcionários da própria Nvidia também contestaram a inclusão de seus nomes na lista, afirmando que não assinaram o documento.

Além da petição, trabalhadores da Nvidia também discutem a possibilidade de organizar uma manifestação em apoio a Huang no campus da companhia, em Santa Clara, na Califórnia, segundo o "The Wall Street Journal".

Por que os apoiadores querem Huang de volta?

Parte dos apoiadores vê Huang como uma peça importante na disputa dos Estados Unidos com a China pelo domínio da inteligência artificial.

➡️ Na avaliação desse grupo, a Nvidia tem papel central no desenvolvimento da tecnologia, já que seus chips são usados para treinar e operar sistemas de IA.

Eles também argumentam que restrições mais rígidas à venda de chips avançados para empresas chinesas podem acabar beneficiando concorrentes locais, como a Huawei.

Investidores pedem que conselho não escolha substituto às pressas

A mobilização também chegou aos investidores da fabricante de chips. Na sexta-feira (13), Brad Gerstner, presidente da gestora Altimeter Capital, e Gavin Baker, da Atreides Management, enviaram uma carta aberta ao conselho da Nvidia.

Os dois defenderam que a companhia não escolha um novo presidente-executivo antes de esclarecer as circunstâncias da saída de Huang. Para eles, o executivo merece um processo cuidadoso, sem uma substituição apressada antes que todos os fatos sejam conhecidos.

💻 A Nvidia foi fundada em 1993 por Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky e Curtis Priem. A companhia se tornou uma das principais fornecedoras mundiais de chips usados no desenvolvimento de inteligência artificial, tecnologia que impulsionou seu crescimento nos últimos anos.

Na sexta-feira, o conselho informou que estava contratando uma empresa especializada em recrutamento para buscar um novo CEO. A Nvidia também afirmou que ainda não havia iniciado conversas formais com possíveis candidatos.

Enquanto isso, a diretora financeira da Nvidia, Colette Kress, ocupa o cargo de presidente-executiva de forma interina.

➡️ Segundo a CNBC, uma pessoa familiarizada com o assunto afirmou que o conselho de administração da Nvidia não discute o retorno de Jensen Huang ao cargo de CEO. De acordo com a fonte, a prioridade da empresa é a investigação sobre a conduta do executivo e possíveis riscos à segurança nacional e a informações sigilosas da companhia.

A saída de Huang ocorreu após a divulgação de relatos sobre dois relacionamentos extraconjugais . Um deles teria envolvido uma empresária de Singapura chamada Alice Huang, ligada à empresa Megaspeed, que atua no setor de data centers e se tornou parceira de negócios da Nvidia.

Autoridades americanas suspeitam que Alice Huang tenha repassado informações à inteligência chinesa durante o relacionamento . A suspeita ainda está sob investigação.

O caso também levantou questionamentos sobre possíveis negócios envolvendo chips da Nvidia e empresas do Sudeste Asiático que atenderiam companhias chinesas. Os Estados Unidos mantêm restrições à venda de determinados semicondutores avançados para a China, por preocupações com segurança nacional e o desenvolvimento de inteligência artificial pelo país.

Além do relacionamento com a empresária, Huang também foi associado a um segundo caso, com uma funcionária da Nvidia que respondia a ele na estrutura da companhia.

Governo americano defende mudança no comando

A tentativa de trazer Huang de volta também enfrenta resistência. O secretário do Tesouro dos Estados Unidos, Scott Bessent, defendeu que a Nvidia procure um executivo de fora da companhia para assumir o comando.

Em entrevista à Fox News, no domingo (15), Bessent afirmou que a empresa precisa de uma mudança significativa. Ele também cobrou explicações sobre a possibilidade de chips da Nvidia terem chegado à China por meio de empresas intermediárias no Sudeste Asiático.

Para o secretário, as dúvidas sobre o cumprimento das regras americanas de exportação precisam ser esclarecidas pela companhia.
