articles.title: Person of interest being questioned by FBI in Illinois ethanol plant bomb investigation
articles.summary: FBI Springfield, Illinois, is leading the manhunt after a credible explosive device was found at BioUrja Renewables in Peoria, sparking evacuations.
articles.body: A person of interest is being questioned Monday in an investigation into who left a bomb near an ethanol facility in Peoria, Illinois, a police spokesperson confirmed to Fox News. The FBI, whose Springfield, Illinois, office is leading the ongoing investigation, confirmed "law enforcement activity" in Peoria County but did not get specific on the questioning. Peoria police had previously said a "person of interest has been taken into custody," but later adjusted that statement. Peoria police redirected all further comment to the FBI Springfield Field Office. "The Peoria Police Department has no further comment at this time," spokesperson Semone Roth said. BOMB FOUND AT PEORIA ETHANOL PLANT PROMPTS EVACUATIONS The explosive device found at BioUrja Renewables on Friday led to evacuations within a one-mile "blast radius" and triggered nearly a 24-hour emergency response. A large facility the size of 44½ football fields and a large area that was evacuated suggested a potentially major threat to public safety. "I can just tell you it was deemed a credible threat," Peoria Police Chief Brad Dixon told reporters at a briefing Saturday, noting that forensic testing is still underway to determine the exact composition of the device. "There's an extensive criminal investigation going on." Dixon declined to call the device a "bomb" despite the facility reporting to police it had received a bomb threat. Authorities warned that because the facility houses large quantities of ethanol and other highly combustible chemicals, an ignition could have triggered a massive explosion far larger than the device itself. IED NEAR ALABAMA RESERVOIR DETONATED AFTER OFFICIALS WARN OF 'UNPRECEDENTED' CRITICAL INFRASTRUCTURE THREAT FBI Special Agent Ryan Presley said the investigation remains in its preliminary stages, declining to release further details about a potential motive or suspect. A Sunday morning news conference held by the Springfield office was postponed until at least Monday. "While the area has been cleared and no additional suspicious devices have been located, the FBI encourages the public to remain alert and share any relevant information they may have," Springfield FBI posted Saturday to X. "We will work tirelessly to identify the individual responsible and bring them to justice," Presley added, noting the FBI has provided bomb technicians, investigative and intelligence resources to local authorities before taking over the lead of the investigation. WAVE OF SCHOOL BOMB THREATS ROCKS KENTUCKY AMID SUSPECTED ROBOCALL SCHEME, POLICE SAY The incident began Friday afternoon when workers at the Peoria plant reported a bomb threat they received to police. Roughly an hour later, crews located a suspicious package near the facility. Peoria Mayor Rita Ali warned of a potentially catastrophic event because, she told WMBD-TV, BioUrja is "a plant that has ethanol and highly combustible types of chemicals, and so that’s what alarms us." By Saturday afternoon, officials from the Peoria Police Department, the FBI and the U.S. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives completed their search of the facility and confirmed no other items of concern were found. Bomb technicians rendered it safe, Peoria police said. The evacuation order was lifted Saturday, almost a full day after the device was discovered Friday close to the ethanol plant in Peoria, a city of about 110,000 people, about 150 miles southwest of Chicago. Bomb technicians rendered it safe, Peoria police said. CAR LOADED WITH EXPLOSIVES SLAMS INTO LAVISH PORTLAND SOCIAL CLUB, BOMB SQUAD STILL PULLING OUT LIVE DEVICES "We understand that this is a disruptive process for our residents and guests," Dixon said. "We’re asking for the public’s patience while we work to make this area safe." No injuries were reported, and no arrests have been made. ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT ALLEGEDLY MADE BOMB THREAT ON FLIGHT, DHS SAYS "#FBISpringfield is now leading the investigation following the identification of an explosive device found at BioUrja Renewables on Friday, Nov. 13," the Saturday X post began. "While the area has been cleared and no additional suspicious devices have been located, the FBI encourages the public to remain alert and share any relevant information they may have related to this ongoing situation by immediately calling 9-1-1, 1-800-CALL-FBI, or online at http:// tips.fbi.gov. "Tipsters may elect to remain anonymous," it added. "The FBI continues to work closely with local, state, and federal law enforcement partners, to include @ATFHQ, @ILSecOfState, @ILStatePolice, the Peoria County Sheriff’s Office, Peoria Fire Department, and @peoria_police, to identify the individual(s) responsible and will hold them fully accountable under the law. All releasable investigative updates will be shared via official FBI Springfield social channels." Because the BioUrja Renewables plant sits directly on the banks of the Illinois River, the one-mile evacuation zone extended across the waterway. Coast Guard Capt. Brandy Parker confirmed the agency established a safety perimeter blocking all vessel traffic between mile markers 160 and 164 while bomb technicians rendered the device safe and searched the facility. The Illinois River, a major tributary of the Mississippi, is a major commercial shipping corridor. The Coast Guard is responsible for securing inland navigable waterways and waterfront industrial facilities against terrorism, sabotage and hazardous material spills — especially given the catastrophic environmental and safety risks if an explosion had ignited the plant's ethanol reserves. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Parker serves as the sector commander for U.S. Coast Guard Sector Upper Mississippi River. The safety shutdown came the same weekend Coast Guard crews far south in Sector New Orleans were forced to close a stretch of the lower Mississippi River after the asphalt tanker Atlantic Asphalt collided with a docked cruise ship carrying 129 passengers near the Port of New Orleans. Fox News' Janelle Benham, The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: Northern Ireland: Westminster budget leaves NI underfunded, O'Dowd says
articles.summary: Northern Ireland's public funding has worsened relative to rest of the UK as a result of the Westminster budget, Stormont's Finance Minister has claimed.
articles.body:
Northern Ireland's public funding has worsened relative to the rest of the UK as a result of the Westminster budget, Stormont's finance minister has claimed.

John O'Dowd said the Treasury's figures show that NI will now be funded below its objective "level of need" next year and the year after.

Needs-based funding recognises that it costs more to deliver public services in some parts of the UK compared to others.

The Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant has offered £1.5bn over the next three years and said if Stormont ministers accept this, that will take funding comfortably above the level of need.

O'Dowd said: "Treasury's own assessment shows that we are underfunded, relative to our current estimate of need, in 2027/28 and 2028/29.

"My officials' analysis also indicates that we are underfunded this year, and therefore in each year of the Spending Review."

It is understood O'Dowd believes that in cash terms this means public services will be underfunded by around £450m over the next three years.

It comes as executive ministers held further talks about the budget deadlock on Monday afternoon at Stormont Castle.

Following the meeting, First Minister Michelle O'Neill said the Secretary of State is "not listening" to the Stormont executive over its continuing budget pressures.

She said their concerns may now need to be "elevated" to the prime minister and warned Andy Burnham that Stormont's political and financial stability were "two sides of the one coin".

She reiterated the executive's argument that Northern Ireland has been significantly "underfunded" in comparison to the devolved governments in Scotland and Wales.

O'Neill said it was "very clear that we have taken this to where we can with the Secretary of State".

Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly said what the executive was asking of the government was "absolutely reasonable".

Speaking after the executive meeting, she said it was "positive that we're continuing to discuss these issues".

"What we are asking the UK government to do is absolutely reasonable, and that is to work with us to try to get a balanced budget to actually fulfil the legal duties that we have," she said.

"We will be doing everything we can in the DUP to support getting that budget settlement to enable us to do public sector pay."

Needs-based funding attempts to give each part of the UK the same quality of public services.

It recognises that public services can be more expensive to deliver in NI because, for example, it has a more rural and dispersed population than in England.

NI is therefore assessed as needing £124 per head for every £100 per head spent on public services in England. This is known as the 124% needs-based funding level.

It is understood the Treasury figures and Department of Finance calculations show NI will be funded at around 123% this year and in the two following years.

How does this impact budget negotiations?

Stormont ministers are currently trying to get more money from the UK government which they say they need to reach a balanced budget.

The secretary of state has offered £1.5bn over the next three years.

Stormont ministers say that is not enough and O'Dowd says the needs-based underfunding makes the situation worse.

"Around one third of the currently proposed financial package from the British government is required on its own to merely bring us to the 124% level of need," he added.

Chris Bryant said that if Stormont ministers accept his offer that will take funding comfortably above the level of need.

"The NI executive has been offered an additional £1.5bn over the next three years, which would mean NI remains funded above 126% in all years of the Spending Review," he said.

"If the executive is to avoid a major public services crisis in the new year it needs to set a budget as a matter of urgency. That is its legal responsibility."

articles.title: 'I may not return alive': Imran Khan asks courts for treatment, says 22-hour isolation is killing him
articles.summary: Pakistan's jailed former prime minister Imran Khan has appealed to the country's top courts for urgent medical treatment for himself and his wife, warning
articles.body: Pakistan's jailed former prime minister Imran Khan has appealed to the country's top courts for urgent medical treatment for himself and his wife, warning that his health has deteriorated to the point where he fears he may not survive.In an open letter, Khan alleged that authorities had ignored earlier court directions on his treatment and described being held in solitary confinement for up to 22 hours a day.The letter, addressed to the chief justices of the Pakistan’s Federal Constitutional Court, the country’s Supreme Court and Islamabad high court, was shared on X by his lawyer Barrister Salman Safdar. Safdar had met Khan at Adiala jail on November 11, when the former prime minister asked him to convey his concerns to the judges.“I spent my life building hospitals so that those who could not afford treatment would receive it free of cost. Today, I ask only that my wife and I be treated,” Khan wrote.Khan claims prolonged isolation has affected his healthIn the letter, Khan alleged that he had been kept disconnected from the outside world, with no access to family members, lawyers, telephone calls to his sons, books or television. He said the isolation had lasted for up to 22 hours a day and had taken a serious toll on his mental health.He claimed that his lawyer had been allowed to meet him only four times during the year, while Bushra Bibi, his wife, had met her counsel just once. Khan also alleged that his weekly meeting with his wife had been skipped without explanation and that he had not been allowed to meet his sisters, who he said were in custody.Khan said a jail medical board had recorded his anxiety and recommended more frequent contact with his wife and family, along with access to reading material and television. He alleged that these recommendations had not been followed.“No one in the jail is permitted to respond to me or speak to me, not when I offer them salaam and not when I recite a verse of the Holy Quran,” he wrote, adding that he believed the restrictions were intended to make him ill and break his will.He also said his lawyer had discovered during a meeting on February 10 that he had lost 85% of the vision in his right eye. According to Khan, neither his family nor his legal counsel had been informed about the condition at the time.Blood pressure readings reached 192 and 193, Khan saysKhan said his blood pressure had risen steadily during his confinement, from 130 to 150 and then 170, before reaching 192 and 193 on November 10.He said doctors had warned him that he was highly vulnerable to a brain haemorrhage and cardiac arrest, and that his heart had already suffered damage.“At seventy-four, this unrelenting state is taking me to a place from which I may not return alive,” he wrote.Khan said he was writing from a solitary cell because it had become “the only way my voice can leave these walls”. He also rejected the suggestion that he was seeking medical relief as a way to avoid his legal cases, saying he had continued to contest them on their merits.Bushra Bibi could lose her eyesight, he saysKhan said his wife's condition was the immediate reason he had decided to write to the courts. According to the letter, Bushra Bibi suffered a retinal detachment in April and underwent what he described as complicated eye surgery in secrecy before being returned to solitary confinement.He said that when he saw her this month, she could neither tolerate light nor open her eyes. Without another operation, he warned, she could lose her sight permanently.Khan alleged that her medical records had been withheld and that she had been denied access to her own doctors. He also raised concerns over her pending request for suspension of sentence.Also check: Two sisters of ex-Pak PM Imran Khan released from jail; elder sister, wife remain behind barsBushra Bibi has separately approached the courts seeking an examination by an ophthalmologist and permission to receive treatment from doctors of her choice at her own expense. She has said doctors diagnosed her with a mature cataract and advised another eye operation.Khan says Pak SC order on hospital transfer was not followedThe former prime minister said the Supreme Court had directed on August 18 that he be shifted to Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad within two days. The order also called for a medical board to examine him and for him to be allowed contact with his family, according to the letter.“That order has not been implemented,” Khan wrote.The government had instead taken him to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences for an eye check-up before returning him to prison. Pakistan’s information minister Attaullah Tarar had attributed the change in arrangements to security concerns linked to PTI workers gathering outside the hospital. The PTI denied the allegations and accused the government of disregarding the court's directions.Khan also complained that his medical concerns were not being heard as promptly as other legal matters, saying his appeal in the Toshakhana-2 case was being taken up ahead of older matters concerning his health and the implementation of court orders.He and Bushra Bibi were sentenced to 17 years in prison in the Toshakhana-2 case, which relates to the purchase of a Bulgari jewellery set gifted to Khan by the Saudi crown prince during an official visit in 2021.Khan said he had faced numerous prosecutions after losing power in a no-confidence vote in 2022, but maintained that he had chosen to fight the cases through the courts. He alleged that the legal system had failed to provide relief when he and his wife needed it most.“I do not ask your Lordships for any favour. All I request as justice is the implementation of the orders of the honourable SC and proper treatment for our medical conditions,” he wrote.He added that he could prove his innocence only if he remained alive, and urged the judges to intervene “before it is too late”.Khan's sons also reacted to the letter. Kasim Khan described it as devastating to read, while Sulaiman Khan called it “incredibly harrowing” and said his father's demand for medical care was not a request for special treatment.Khan has been in prison since August 2023. Bushra Bibi was arrested in January 2025 in a separate case. Khan denies wrongdoing in the corruption cases against him and says they are politically motivated. articles.title: Landmark Crimea bridge hit as Russia reports biggest Ukrainian drone attack of war
articles.summary: Russia said Ukraine had launched over 2,000 drones over the course of a day, while Kyiv came under a record 17 air raid alerts.
articles.body:
Russia says it has recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, in which a landmark bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea sustained minor damage and several oil refineries were hit.

The Russian military intercepted and destroyed 2,049 drones and four Flamingo long-distance missiles over 24 hours, officials said. Around 600 flew towards capital alone, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin added.

Kyiv, meanwhile, came under a record 17 air raid alerts in a single day. At least seven people were killed by Russian strikes and attacks on energy infrastructure caused blackouts for 50,000 people.

The intense strikes come days after US, Ukrainian and Russian envoys held talks aimed at ending the war.

The war in Ukraine began with Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

The Moscow-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, confirmed that drones had struck the Crimean Bridge connecting Russia with the annexed peninsula, leading to traffic restrictions.

The structure - also known as Kerch Bridge - was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014. It was inaugurated by Russian President Vladimir Putin to great fanfare in 2018 and is carefully protected with multiple layers of aerial and maritime defences.

Russian pro-war military commentators said on Telegram that rather than a direct attack, the bridge had suffered from the impact of drone warhead debris. Neither Ukraine's domestic security service nor its main military intelligence directorate has responded to a BBC request for comment.

Atesh, a partisan Ukrainian group operating inside Russian-held territory, said on social media that authorities in Crimea were "bracing for further strikes" on the Kerch Bridge and that they felt Moscow did not appreciate the seriousness of the situation.

Ukrainian drones also hit several energy facilities, including an oil refinery in Ilsky, in the southern Krasnodar region, where falling drone debris sparked a fire and injured six people, including children.

Last week, President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Russia of carrying out a concerted operation against Ukraine's bridges in order to "divide Ukraine... and make life as difficult as possible for people" on both sides of the Dnipro River which cuts across the country.

Despite the high-level diplomacy and visits by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff to both Putin and Zelensky, peace remains a distant prospect.

Moscow is uncompromising on its demands for Ukraine to cede territory and give up efforts to become a Nato member.

The Kremlin has now also started to talk again about the need to rethink Europe's "security architecture", often intended by Moscow to mean a scaled-down Nato presence in countries close to Russia.

The apparent willingness of the US to engage in this conversation has set off alarm bells among Ukraine's European partners, which are concerned their continent's security could be redrawn by Washington and Moscow without their involvement.

A team of six - Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Poland and a representative of the EU institutions - will represent Europe in future talks with Russia, Ukraine and the US.

But the Kremlin continues to be dismissive of European input.

"We have also said more than once we need to understand... how much their position will help the peace process," said spokesman Dmitri Peskov.

EU representatives kept pushing for "unconditional support" for Ukraine and "enhanced pressure" on Russia, Peskov said, adding that "this sort of wording rather suggests their reluctance to facilitate the peace process".

articles.title: Trump border crackdown drives encounters to record October low as zero-release streak hits 18 months, DHS says
articles.summary: Border Patrol recorded just 8,288 southwest border apprehensions in October, marking a stunning 95% drop from the Biden administration's average.
articles.body: Border Patrol agents caught fewer illegal immigrants at the southwest border in all of October than they did in just five days of the same month under former President Joe Biden in 2024, according to new federal figures. The sharp drop comes as the Trump administration reports 18 straight months of zero releases at the border and the lowest nationwide encounter total ever recorded for the opening month of a fiscal year. "President Trump unleashed the full strength of DHS to secure the border and enforce the law," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said. "The results speak for themselves." TRUMP DHS HITS 16 STRAIGHT MONTHS WITH 0 RELEASES AT THE BORDER "Under President Trump’s leadership, we will continue to deliver the most secure border in American history and save American lives," Mullin added. Border Patrol recorded 8,288 apprehensions along the southwest border in October, down 95% from the Biden administration’s monthly average and 97% from its December 2023 peak, according to the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Customs and Border Protection. TRUMP ADMIN MARKS 15 STRAIGHT MONTHS WITH ZERO BORDER RELEASES AS APPREHENSIONS PLUNGE 94% The numbers stand in sharp contrast to the surge retired Yuma Sector Border Patrol Chief Chris Clem described in an October interview with Fox News Digital, when he recalled overwhelmed agents and migrants spilling into surrounding communities. "They just started walking through the agriculture fields. They started running through town," Clem said, recalling December 2021. "They started going to the food bank. They started knocking on people’s doors at all hours of the night." CBS REPORT MARVELS AT ONCE-CHAOTIC SOUTHERN BORDER CROSSING HAS GONE QUIET UNDER TRUMP CRACKDOWN In Yuma alone, Clem said daily arrivals climbed from roughly 25 in December 2020 to more than 1,000 a year later. During one particularly difficult three-day stretch in December 2021, daily arrivals approached 1,500, he said. "The agents, their heads were in the right place. They knew they had to do the job," Clem said. "But when you’re outnumbered, literally 100 to one, it’s very difficult." DHS TOUTS MILLIONS OF ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT DEPARTURES AS BORDER CROSSINGS DROP 94% UNDER TRUMP The latest southwest border apprehension total fell 7% from September, carrying the decline into the first month of fiscal year 2027. Nationwide, CBP recorded 27,890 encounters in October, also down 7% from September. That was the lowest October total on record and the lowest for any month since February, the agencies said. TRUMP HITS DRAMATIC MILESTONE IN MASSIVE DEPARTURE FROM BIDEN BORDER PLAN: 'WHAT A DIFFERENCE' The new figures follow preliminary DHS data showing 98,708 southwest border apprehensions for all of fiscal year 2026, roughly 95% below the Biden administration’s annual average of more than 1.8 million. Clem credited stronger border enforcement and the prospect of deportation with changing the calculation for people considering crossing illegally. TRUMP ADMINISTRATION'S IMMIGRATION PUSH FUELS ICE'S BIGGEST ARREST MONTH IN AGENCY HISTORY "They know that they’re not gonna be processed and released, which was the status quo under the Biden-Harris administration," he told Fox News Digital in the October interview. He said enforcement inside the country reinforced that message by making clear that getting past Border Patrol did not eliminate the possibility of arrest and removal. ICE ARRESTS MORE THAN 100 ALLEGED GANG MEMBERS IN SINGLE WEEK, INCLUDING VIOLENT MS-13, TDA SUSPECTS: DHS "When you combine the strong border posture, as well as the strong and robust interior enforcement, it’s a recipe for success," Clem said. CBP Commissioner Rodney S. Scott credited Trump and Mullin with giving the agency an "unprecedented level of control over our borders." MULLIN TELLS RUTHLESS PODCAST THAT THE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION HAS APPREHENDED 2,210 TERRORISTS "We know more about who and what is entering our homeland than at any time in our nation’s history," Scott said in the latest announcement. "America is safer because we are enforcing the rule of law, keeping threats out of our communities and putting the security of the American people first," he added. The decline in border apprehensions came as CBP reported a jump in the weight of drugs seized nationwide. Seizures of cocaine, methamphetamine, heroin, fentanyl and marijuana collectively rose 44% from September, according to the agencies. Officers and agents seized 14,745 pounds of methamphetamine and 9,032 pounds of cocaine in October, increases of 59% and 60%, respectively. The release did not include a separate October total for fentanyl. Still, Clem cautioned in October that lower apprehension numbers did not eliminate threats from smugglers or people trying to evade detection. "There are always gonna be that risk where somebody does sneak through. Who is that person?" he said. "We have an immigration issue we need to address," Clem said. "We need to find a way to retain and recruit those that are here, that are foreign nationals that want to contribute." articles.title: Robert Pattinson: How the Twilight star became 007
articles.summary: The Twilight, Batman and Odyssey star's profile will go even more stellar when he plays James Bond.
articles.body:
Robert Pattinson's career is already flying high with roles in films including the Twilight series, The Batman and The Odyssey, so signing up to play James Bond will propel his profile into the stratosphere.

He's already established himself as a leading man, action star and character actor, which is clearly why he is about to play the suave, British secret agent 007.

At 40, he is slightly older than some of the other men reportedly lined up for the role , but he's also the most famous - something the new Bond studio Amazon-MGM may have favoured, with an eye on the box office.

His recent work has garnered both critical and box office success, including Christopher Nolan's summer blockbuster The Odyssey, in which he played the villainous Antinous.

Pattinson was also called "Oscar-worthy" by the Independent and "superb" by The Times, for his performance in November's Primetime, as the real-life host of US TV show To Catch a Predator.

He also helped lead 2022's The Batman to the second-biggest North American opening of the Covid-19 pandemic behind Spider-Man: No Way Home. The Guardian said he played the "brooding" role with " appealing vulnerability ".

Meanwhile in dark romantic comedy The Drama, he and his co-star gave a "career-highlight performance" . It's one of three films he appeared in with Zendaya this year, along with The Odyssey and Dune: Part Three.

Born in Barnes, south-west London, Pattinson grew up with his father, a classic car trader and mother, who worked at a modelling agency, and two elder sisters.

His interest in acting started while he was still at school, when he joined the Barnes Theatre Club.

"I wouldn't be acting if it wasn't for that little club," he told Your Local Guardian in 2008 .

"I went originally because a lot of pretty girls went there," he said. "I worked backstage and I started acting when all the good people left and I was the only one tall enough to play the lead.

"In a weird sort of way, that stuff was probably the best I've done and the stuff I am most proud of."

He landed his first big film role more than two decades ago, playing Cedric Diggory in 2005's Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire. A relatively minor character, but it was enough to get him noticed.

Three years later, he had a starring role in the first of five Twilight films, along with Kristen Stewart, in which they played star-crossed lovers - vampire Edward Cullen and mortal-turned vampire Kristen Stewart.

Based on Stephanie Meyer's hugely popular young adult books, the films globally grossed more than $3bn (£2.2bn) by 2012, and established Pattinson as a heartthrob.

He spoke in his early career of finding his often adoring, screaming fans hard to deal with.

"Although is part of the job, it feels like they have been paid to turn up and scream at me at 7.30pm," he said.

"Nothing I don't think can prepare you for the fans. I don't know why I'm not getting used to it but I'm completely overwhelmed every time."

In 2010, Time included him in their list of 100 people who "most affect our world" , saying perhaps prophetically that "we haven't seen a tenth of what he can do on screen".

After such mainstream success with the Twilight franchise, Pattinson was able to branch out.

He went on to work with several acclaimed independent film directors including David Cronenberg, starring in his film Cosmpopolis in 2012, as well as working with Werner Herzog in 2015's Queen of the Desert and The Lighthouse (2019), directed by Robert Eggers.

Pattinson told Screen Daily why he took the role in psychological horror film The Lighthouse , saying he told Eggers: "I just want to do something weird."

The following year though, he was back in big-studio territory, with Odyssey director Christopher Nolan, in sci-fi thriller Tenet, and again in 2022 with The Batman, directed by Matt Reeves and co-starring Zoe Kravitz and Paul Dano.

Pattinson told Screen Daily why he returned to big-budget films, explaining: "I guess I was trying to do the opposite of what I've been doing. I started thinking, 'I really want to do a big thing.'

"I hadn't done something with a massive budget for ages. But you approach it exactly the same way."

The Batman got generally positive reviews, re-establishing Pattinson with a broader range of fans.

By 2025, when he was on the red carpet for Parasite director Bong Joon Ho's sci-fi black comedy, Mickey 17, he said it was "quite strange" to have a fanbase that was now dominated by men .

"There's like a bunch of guys, which is a new one for me!" he told the Associated Press.

Pattinson's private life has often created interest in the press, not least his previous relationships with Stewart, and then the singer FKA Twigs.

Since 2018, he has been in a relationship with model Suki Waterhouse. They got engaged in December 2023 and had their first child, a daughter, in March.

With his latest role as James Bond, Pattinson will be extremely busy, not least because the forthcoming Batman sequel is reportedly due out in 2028.

But the actor will have a head start as 007, having already worked with Bond 26 director Denis Villeneuve, who also helmed Dune: Part Three.

Pattinson was full of praise for him on their most recent film, despite the strain of working in the furnace-like heat of the desert.

"The scale of this stuff is just unbelievable, you're having your own Dune theme park, where the gimbal is going upside down and flying, and this is not like work at all," he told the New York Times .

"There are no negatives. Apart from having your sweat drained out of the top of your head, and getting like bulbous sweat bubbles. But even then, I didn't even really notice them.

"He's so easy to work with, Denis, it's never really a stress."

Sounds like Pattinson will have the cool head needed to juggle his forthcoming roles - including James Bond. You could even say he may end up being shaken, but not stirred.

articles.title: Obama did it, Biden did it, Trump follows suit: Why US presidents head abroad after poll defeats
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump is heading to Asia after a setback for Republicans in the midterm elections, following a pattern adopted by several of his
articles.body: US President Donald Trump is heading to Asia after a setback for Republicans in the midterm elections, following a pattern adopted by several of his predecessors. From Ronald Reagan and Bill Clinton to George W Bush and Barack Obama, US presidents have used overseas trips after electoral setbacks to shift attention to foreign policy and project their authority on the global stage.Trump’s trip will take him to the Philippines and China for the ASEAN and APEC summits. The agenda includes meetings with regional leaders, trade agreements and an unprecedented trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin to discuss nuclear weapons. The visit comes as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress and questions grow over how much political room Trump will have at home.The practice of taking foreign trips after domestic political setbacks is not new. It dates back to 1982, when Reagan travelled to Latin America after Republicans suffered losses in the midterm elections. Since then, several presidents have followed a similar approach, using international engagements to reinforce the office of the presidency even as their political position at home comes under pressure.A foreign policy stage after setbacks at homeThe strategy is aimed at shifting the focus from domestic political troubles to the president’s role in international affairs. Foreign visits offer opportunities for high-profile meetings, public appearances and announcements that underline the president's position as the country's representative abroad.“Foreign policy and presidential trips are something only the president can do. There is pomp and circumstance. There’s a focus on it,” CNN quoted Edgard Kagan, a former US ambassador to Malaysia and senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, as saying. “This is a way in which you start changing the narrative, and remind people that, you know, the president is still the president.”Kagan said such trips also remind foreign governments that the president remains central to US foreign policy.For Trump, the Asia visit offers an opportunity to announce commercial deals and reinforce US engagement in a region where Washington has long sought to maintain its influence. The trip also comes against the backdrop of the Iran war and the ongoing conflict in Ukraine, both of which continue to shape his foreign policy agenda.From Reagan to Obama: The pattern takes shapeThe approach is traced back to Reagan's 1982 trip to Latin America. At the time, the US was dealing with a recession and unemployment of 11%, while Democrats had gained 26 seats in the House of Representatives in the midterm elections.Reagan's five-day visit was organised by his adviser Michael Deaver, who is credited with developing the idea of using an overseas tour to change the political narrative after an election setback.Bill Clinton followed the pattern in November 1994, travelling to the Philippines after Republicans won control of both chambers of Congress. In 2006, George W Bush visited Vietnam and other countries in Asia within weeks of Republicans losing control of the House and Senate.Barack Obama also travelled to Asia after the Democrats suffered midterm losses in 2010 and 2014. In 2010, Democrats lost control of the House, a setback Obama described as a “shellacking”.Trump himself made a visit to France in 2017 after Republicans lost their majority in the House.Biden's 2024 trip came after election defeatJoe Biden's six-day visit to Peru and Brazil in November 2024 came days after Donald Trump defeated Kamala Harris in the presidential election. The trip included the APEC summit in Peru and the G20 summit in Brazil, as well as meetings with several world leaders, including Xi Jinping. It was among Biden's final major international engagements before leaving office in January 2025.While Biden's trip followed a presidential election defeat rather than a midterm loss, it also placed him on the international stage at a time when the incoming administration's policies were already drawing attention from foreign governments.Why Trump's trip carries added significanceTrump's visit comes at a time when his domestic political position is facing fresh scrutiny. Republicans lost both chambers of Congress in the midterms, while Democrats are preparing to use their incoming majority to investigate the administration.The trip also comes amid controversy surrounding Nvidia and its chief executive Jensen Huang, following reports of an alleged link to a Chinese government agent. US officials have said Trump does not intend to raise the matter with Xi during their meeting.The trilateral meeting with Xi and Putin is another major focus. While Putin had proposed the meeting as a forum to discuss the Ukraine war, Trump's aides have said Ukraine will not be on the agenda. Instead, the US president wants to open discussions on nuclear weapons.The US and Russia each have an estimated 5,000 nuclear warheads, while China's arsenal has grown to more than 600. The last nuclear arms treaty between Washington and Moscow expired in February.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Pregnant US citizen pepper-sprayed, thrown to ground on stomach by ICE agents in California; video shows husband warning ‘she's pregnant’
articles.summary: A pregnant US citizen was pepper-sprayed, forced face-down onto the pavement and then handcuffed by federal immigration agents during a confrontation
articles.body: A pregnant US citizen was pepper-sprayed, forced face-down onto the pavement and then handcuffed by federal immigration agents during a confrontation outside a California county jail, according to her lawyer and video footage of the incident. Lizbeth Vargas Andrade, 23, who is 12 weeks pregnant, was detained by ICE agents outside the Stanislaus County Jail in Modesto on Sunday while officers were attempting to take another person into custody, her attorney Patrick Kolasinski said.The video showed plainclothes federal agents wearing tactical vests marked "POLICE" and "FEDERAL AGENT" surrounding a silver minivan in a parking lot. Andrade approached one of the agents while recording the encounter on her phone.The agent grabbed her arm as another officer moved in to restrain her. The second agent then pulled out a red canister of pepper spray and pointed it towards another woman and the person recording the confrontation.Andrade's husband, Adolfo Talavera, can be heard warning the agents that she was pregnant."She's pregnant with child," he told them.Despite the warning, two agents forced Andrade face-down onto the pavement beside a black SUV and handcuffed her with her hands behind her back. An agent later rolled her onto her side and helped her into a seated position. The footage also showed an agent pouring water from a plastic jug over her face."Lizbeth Vargas Andrade, a pregnant US citizen, was pepper sprayed, thrown to the ground on her stomach, and arrested by ICE agents while participating in a protest outside the Stanislaus County Jail," her lawyer said.Who is Andrade? What happened before the confrontation?Andrade said she had been monitoring immigration enforcement activity in California's Central Valley and began livestreaming on TikTok after spotting federal agents outside the jail.The confrontation unfolded as ICE agents attempted to detain someone who had just been released from the county jail. It remained unclear who the agents were initially looking for or what that person's immigration or criminal history was.Andrade's husband said at a news conference on Sunday that he, his wife and his sister, Monica Alvarado, were all pepper-sprayed during the encounter. Alvarado was driving the minivan that was stopped by immigration agents.Andrade denied an agent's allegation that she had assaulted him. She said they had bumped into each other before officers took her to the ground. She also said she hit her stomach during the takedown.Following the confrontation, Andrade was taken to an ICE field office in Stockton, California, although she said she was not formally processed there. Her sister called an ambulance, which transported Andrade, who is diabetic, to a hospital. She said two immigration agents remained with her during the hospital visit and that she was denied access to an attorney.Andrade was released on Sunday night after spending several hours in federal custody, her lawyer said. She was not charged with a crime.Speaking after her release, Andrade said neither she nor her pregnancy had suffered harm.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Cargo ship capsizes off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast
articles.summary: Bulgaria’s Transport Ministry says that all 12 of the ship’s crew members were saved in a rescue operation.
articles.body:
A cargo ship has capsized off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast, the country’s Transport Ministry has said.

The ship’s crew, eight Turkish citizens and four Azerbaijani nationals, were rescued from the Somali-flagged Betul 8 in an operation on Monday that involved four ships, two from Bulgaria, one from Romania and one from Turkiye.

Bulgaria’s Transport Ministry confirmed that one of its helicopters repatriated them to shore and that the crew was in good health.

Speaking to journalists after being brought to the port city of Varna, crew members said their ship had been hit by two sea drones.

The incident comes after three ships were hit off Romania over the weekend, according to authorities in Bucharest, though no casualties were reported.

Romanian Foreign Minister Dan Neculaescu said on Monday the latest incidents were “unacceptable”.

The ship was carrying 3,000 metric tons of wheat and was headed to Egypt from Romania. Bulgaria received a distress signal early on Monday that the ship was sinking approximately 40 nautical miles (74km) southeast of Cape Kaliakra.

Betul 8 is the 17th vessel to be attacked off the coasts of Bulgaria and Romania since mid-July, according to Diaplous, a maritime security firm.

The waters off the coasts of the two countries, both of them NATO members, have become the primary route for shipments from Ukraine, one of the world’s largest grain exporters, whose own Black Sea ports have come under fire since Russia’s full-scale invasion more than four years ago. Ukraine has also been accused of targeting Russian vessels in other areas of the Black Sea.

Romanian and Bulgarian officials have both pointed the finger at Russia over the attacks, though Bulgaria has underlined that there is no proof of who was behind them. Russia has previously denied it was responsible for deadly drone attacks in the region.

articles.title: Customer's restaurant receipt sparks controversy after $6 charge appears for to-go box
articles.summary: STATS restaurant and bar in Charlotte, North Carolina, claims a viral $6 to-go box fee was actually a price adjustment tied to its half-price pasta deal.
articles.body: A North Carolina restaurant is responding to controversy after a customer shared a receipt on social media that appeared to show a $6 charge for a to-go box. STATS, a restaurant and bar in Charlotte, claims the charge was not for a takeout container but was instead a price adjustment tied to its weekly pasta promotion. The restaurant offers half-price pasta on Wednesdays, but the deal is available exclusively to customers dining inside the establishment. RESTAURANT CHAIN MAY RETHINK CONTROVERSIAL 20% SERVICE CHARGE IN SOME VENUES AFTER CUSTOMER PUSHBACK "However, if guests order dine-in promotional items for carry-out, the meal is adjusted to its regular price," STATS said in a statement shared with Fox News Digital. "In this case, the additional $6 was not a charge for a to-go container, but a computer adjustment to that original price." The receipt shared on social media shows a $28 charge for Cajun Alfredo, as well as a $6 charge for the to-go box and a 3% service fee in the amount of $1.02. A representative for STATS also provided additional details about the customer's order, saying the pasta included several extras. "The customer also added two proteins (shrimp and fried salmon) and an additional vegetable (broccoli) to the pasta, which contributed to the overall cost of the dish," the representative told Fox News Digital. "The $6 adjustment was for requesting a dine-in special as carryout." WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS ARE CHANGING DINING AS CUSTOMERS EAT HALF THEIR MEALS, TAKE REST HOME, CELEBRITY CHEF SAYS But the customer clarified on social media that she frequents STATS and didn't go there "with the intention of getting a to-go meal at a cheaper price." "I did not finish my pasta," she wrote. "Because I didn't finish my pasta, I got charged for a box or regular price, however you want to look at it. God forbid a girl gets full." Fox News Digital reached out to the customer for comment. STATS acknowledged that its receipts may have contributed to confusion surrounding the charge and said changes are coming. "We also commit to clearly explaining our gratuity and promotional guidelines to guests."
